title: Musculoskeletal Changes During Pregnancy, Labour and Puerperium
path: Musculoskeletal Changes During Pregnancy, Labour and Puerperium

headings.title: Introduction to Musculoskeletal Adaptations in Pregnancy
headings.content: Musculoskeletal adaptations during pregnancy are profound physiological changes designed to accommodate the growing fetus, prepare the maternal body for birth, and maintain daily functioning. From the moment of conception, the maternal skeletal, muscular, and ligamentous systems undergo continuous remodeling. These changes are not isolated; they affect maternal posture, gait, and joint stability. For student nurses practicing in Nigeria, understanding these normal physiological alterations is crucial for differentiating between expected discomforts of pregnancy and pathological musculoskeletal conditions. Hormonal surges, mechanical loading, and shifts in body weight all combine to alter the biomechanics of the pregnant woman. Recognizing these shifts helps the nurse provide holistic antenatal education, ensuring expectant mothers understand why certain aches occur and how to manage them safely. Furthermore, inadequate recognition of these changes can lead to misdiagnoses of severe back pain or mobility issues. The musculoskeletal system must recover completely during the puerperium, making baseline knowledge of pregnancy-related adaptations foundational for both prenatal and postnatal care.

headings.title: Hormonal Influences: Relaxin, Progesterone, and Joint Laxity
headings.content: Hormonal shifts during pregnancy are the primary drivers of joint laxity and structural flexibility. Two key hormones, relaxin and progesterone, play pivotal roles in this process. Relaxin, produced by the corpus luteum and later the placenta, remodels collagen and causes connective tissue relaxation throughout the body. While its most dramatic effects are seen in the pelvic ligaments, relaxin affects all peripheral joints, increasing the risk of sprains and strains. Progesterone also contributes to smooth muscle relaxation and generalized joint laxity. This systemic relaxation is essential because it allows the pelvis to widen and adapt to the passage of the fetus during delivery. However, the downside of this physiological adaptation is a decrease in joint stability. Pregnant women often experience clumsiness or a feeling of looseness in their weight-bearing joints. Nurses must educate patients that this increased joint laxity makes them more prone to injuries, advising them to avoid high-impact exercises or heavy lifting that could compromise joint integrity. Understanding the timeline of these hormones helps explain why joint discomfort often peaks in the later trimesters when hormone levels are highest and mechanical loads are greatest.

headings.title: Postural Adjustments and Center of Gravity Shifts
headings.content: As the uterus expands anteriorly, the maternal center of gravity shifts forward and upward. To maintain balance and prevent falling forward, the pregnant woman instinctively adopts postural adjustments. The most notable adjustment is leaning backward from the hips and shoulders, creating a compensation pattern that alters the entire kinetic chain. This shift places an immense mechanical burden on the spine, pelvis, and lower extremities. The feet may flatten, and the base of support widens, leading to a characteristic waddling gait often observed in the third trimester. Nursing assessments should include observing the client's posture and gait during antenatal visits. Nurses can guide patients on proper body mechanics, encouraging flat, supportive footwear rather than high heels, which exacerbate the forward center of gravity shift. Awareness of these postural changes helps explain why pregnant women tire easily when standing for long periods. By teaching safe posture and ergonomic principles, nurses can significantly reduce the incidence of musculoskeletal fatigue and strain in expectant mothers.

headings.title: Spinal Changes: Lordosis and Back Pain Etiology
headings.content: To compensate for the forward shift in the center of gravity, the lumbar spine curves inward excessively, a condition known as gestational lordosis. This exaggerated spinal curvature shifts the weight back over the lower limbs, but it places intense pressure on the lumbar vertebrae, facet joints, and supporting paraspinal muscles. Consequently, lower back pain (backache) is one of the most common complaints reported by pregnant women. The etiology of this pain is multifactorial, involving mechanical strain, muscle fatigue, ligamentous laxity induced by relaxin, and stretching of the abdominal wall muscles. As the rectus abdominis muscles separate (diastasis recti), they lose their ability to properly support the spine, worsening the lordotic posture. Nurses play a vital role in assessing the severity of back pain and teaching non-pharmacological relief strategies such as pelvic tilt exercises, prenatal yoga, warm compresses, and proper sitting ergonomics. Distinguishing between normal mechanical back pain and potential complications like preterm labor contractions or pyelonephritis is a critical competency for nursing students providing comprehensive maternal care.

headings.title: Pelvic Girdle Relaxation and Symphysis Pubis Dysfunction
headings.content: Pelvic girdle relaxation is a normal physiological process, but when it becomes excessive or asymmetrical, it results in Symphysis Pubis Dysfunction (SPD) or pelvic girdle pain (PGP). The pubic symphysis and sacroiliac joints experience dramatic increases in mobility due to relaxin and the physical weight of the fetus. In SPD, the joints of the pelvis become overly mobile, causing sharp, debilitating pain in the pubic region, groin, hips, and lower back. Activities that involve unilateral leg loading, such as climbing stairs, getting out of a car, or turning over in bed, frequently exacerbate this pain. Nursing interventions focus on educating the client on joint protection strategies. Nurses should advise patients to keep their knees together when getting out of bed or entering a vehicle, avoid heavy lifting, and utilize pelvic support belts when recommended by a physiotherapist or physician. Early identification of SPD prevents chronic postpartum pelvic pain and improves the quality of life for the expectant mother throughout her pregnancy journey.

headings.title: Lower Extremity Changes: Edema, Cramps, and Gait Alterations
headings.content: Lower extremity changes during pregnancy encompass physiological edema, muscle cramps, and gait alterations. Dependent edema is common in the lower extremities during the later stages of pregnancy due to increased venous pressure in the lower limbs, caused by the gravid uterus compressing the inferior vena cava. Additionally, nocturnal leg cramps frequently plague pregnant women, often linked to imbalances in calcium, magnesium, or phosphorus, as well as circulatory sluggishness and muscle fatigue. Gait alterations, characterized by a wider base of support and a swaying waddle, stem from a combination of joint laxity, increased weight, and shifting center of gravity. Nurses should educate clients on preventive measures for edema and cramps, such as avoiding prolonged standing, elevating the legs frequently, staying well-hydrated, and performing gentle calf stretches before bedtime. It is also vital for the nurse to assess for signs of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), such as unilateral leg swelling, redness, and warmth, to rule out pathological vascular complications.

headings.title: Musculoskeletal Mechanics During Labour and Delivery
headings.content: During labour and delivery, the musculoskeletal system undergoes extreme mechanical stress. The pelvic bones and joints, primed by months of hormonal relaxation, must yield to allow the descent and rotation of the fetus through the birth canal. The pelvic outlet can expand slightly because the coccyx is mobile, pivoting backward as the fetal head passes. Maternal positioning during labour greatly influences pelvic dimensions and comfort. Upright positions, squatting, kneeling, and side-lying maximize pelvic outlet diameters and utilize gravity to assist fetal descent. Conversely, prolonged recumbent or lithotomy positions can compress maternal blood vessels and increase musculoskeletal strain. Nurses play a crucial role during labour by assisting with frequent position changes, supporting the laboring mother's back and limbs, and ensuring proper alignment to prevent nerve compression or muscle injury. Post-delivery, the nurse must assess for signs of acute musculoskeletal trauma, such as symphysis pubis rupture or severe pelvic joint injury resulting from rapid or instrument-assisted deliveries.

headings.title: Postpartum Puerperium: Involution and Recovery of the Musculoskeletal System
headings.content: The puerperium, or postpartum period, is a time of systemic involution and musculoskeletal recovery. Following delivery, hormone levels—specifically relaxin and progesterone—drop precipitously, initiating the gradual return of joint stability and ligamentous tone. However, this recovery process is not instantaneous; joint laxity can persist for several weeks postpartum, leaving new mothers vulnerable to musculoskeletal injuries while caring for their newborns. Diastasis recti may also persist, requiring targeted postpartum abdominal exercises to close the muscle gap and restore core strength. The spine slowly returns from its lordotic curve to its pre-pregnant alignment, though poor lifting mechanics while handling the baby can perpetuate back pain. Nurses providing postnatal care must assess maternal recovery, encourage early safe ambulation to prevent thromboembolism, and teach safe lifting techniques for infant care. Educational topics should include pelvic floor rehabilitation (Kegel exercises) and gradual exercise reintroduction to support total musculoskeletal healing.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Management of Pregnancy-Related Musculoskeletal Discomforts
headings.content: Nursing assessment and management of pregnancy-related musculoskeletal discomforts require a comprehensive, empathetic approach. The nurse should perform targeted assessments during antenatal and postnatal visits, asking about the location, severity, and functional impact of back pain, pelvic girdle pain, and leg cramps. Physical assessment includes checking posture, gait, spinal alignment, and palpating tender joint areas. Management strategies are primarily non-pharmacological, focusing on patient education, lifestyle modifications, and comfort measures. Nurses teach proper ergonomics, such as bending at the knees rather than the waist, using supportive pillows while sleeping, wearing flat shoes, and applying heat or cold packs to sore muscles. Safe exercise recommendations, including prenatal yoga, swimming, and pelvic tilt exercises, are provided to maintain muscle tone. Furthermore, the nurse must recognize when discomfort crosses into the realm of pathology—such as severe incapacitating SPD or signs of nerve impingement like sciatica—and refer the client to physical therapy or obstetric evaluation promptly.
